title: Sharpe, Sortino and Information Ratios
objectives: Compute the Sharpe ratio from a return series, a risk-free rate and a volatility estimate
Compute the Sortino ratio using only downside deviations below a target
Compute the information ratio from active returns and tracking error
Choose the appropriate ratio for a given comparison and state what each one ignores
motivation: Two funds both made 12% last year. One took 8% volatility to get there, the other 25%. Raw returns cannot rank them; risk-adjusted ratios can. These three ratios are the vocabulary of every performance review, fund fact sheet and job interview, so you must be able to compute and critique each one.

blocks.text: Sharpe ratio: excess return per unit of total risk

blocks.caption: Mean excess return divided by the standard deviation of returns (same frequency for all three)

blocks.md: The denominator is *total* volatility, the strategy may be punished for upside surprises too, which is the ratio's best-known blind spot. Sharpe ratios from monthly data are annualised by multiplying by $\sqrt{12}$ (from data at frequency $f$ per year, scale by $\sqrt{f}$). Beware comparisons across frequencies without scaling, and remember the ratio assumes returns are roughly symmetric, fat left tails make Sharpe flatter to deceive.

blocks.title: Worked example: Sharpe from eight hypothetical monthly returns (%)
items: Deviations from the mean: $[2, -3, 1, -2, 3, -1, 0, 0]$; squared deviations sum to $4+9+1+4+9+1+0+0 = 28$.
Risk-free rate $r_f = 0.5\%$ per month, so mean excess return $= 1.0\%$.

blocks.text: Sortino ratio: penalise only the downside

blocks.caption: MAR is the minimum acceptable return (often $r_f$); $\sigma_D$ is the downside deviation

blocks.md: Only returns below MAR enter $\sigma_D$ - upside volatility is free. Continuing the same series with MAR $= 0.5\%$: the shortfalls come from $-1.5$ (shortfall $-2.0$) and $-0.5$ (shortfall $-1.0$); the other six months meet or beat MAR. Sum of squared shortfalls $= 4 + 1 = 5$; divided by $n = 8$ gives $0.625$, so $\sigma_D = \sqrt{0.625} \approx 0.791\%$. Sortino $= 1.0 / 0.791 \approx \textbf{1.26}$ - roughly $2.5\times$ the Sharpe, because this series' volatility lives mostly on the upside.

blocks.title: Why divide by n, not n-1, for Sortino
blocks.md: Conventions differ, but the common estimator uses the full $n$ so that $\sigma_D$ is comparable across funds regardless of how many months fell below MAR. Whatever you pick, state it, a Sortino computed on a different denominator is not comparable to anyone else's.

blocks.text: Information ratio: skill against a benchmark

blocks.caption: Active return over tracking error; the Sharpe ratio of the benchmark-relative game
Sharpe is mean over deviation; Sortino only counts the downside tail. Same history, different denominator: the ratios disagree exactly when the tails matter.

blocks.md: Each ratio in this lesson is a single idea, *reward per unit of a specific pain*, and the specific pain is what distinguishes them. Sharpe divides by total volatility: it penalises upside and downside alike. Sortino divides by downside only, which is what investors actually dislike. The information ratio divides by *active* risk and answers a different question entirely: not "is this portfolio good?" but "is this manager good at deviating from the benchmark?"

blocks.title: All three ratios, one 8-day sample (hypothetical daily returns)
items: Mean $= 1.00\%$/day, standard deviation $= 1.22\%$. Sharpe (rf = 0, annualised by $\sqrt{252}$): $\frac{1.00}{1.22}\sqrt{252} \approx 13.0$, the annualisation makes daily numbers look spectacular, which is exactly why you must check the horizon before comparing any two Sharpes.

Only two days were negative ($-1.0, -0.6$): downside deviation $= \sqrt{(1.0^2 + 0.6^2)/8} = 0.41\%$. Sortino $= \frac{1.00}{0.41}\sqrt{252} \approx 38.5$. The Sortino > Sharpe gap widens as returns skew positive, a rough skewness indicator you get for free.

Active returns (strategy − benchmark) average $0.12\%$/day with tracking error $0.82\%$: information ratio $= \frac{0.12}{0.82}\sqrt{252} \approx 2.42$. An IR above 1 sustained over years is elite; most active managers live near 0.5.
Sanity note: 8 observations make every number here a coin flip. The arithmetic is the lesson, not the values.

rows: skill per unit of benchmark deviation

blocks.title: The denominator can be gamed
blocks.md: Sharpe rises if you add assets with positively-skewed, rare-crash payoffs (short vol, carry): the volatility denominator barely sees the tail. This is why "high Sharpe" strategies blow up, the ratio measured the visible pain, not the real pain. Sortino, Calmar and stress tests exist to look where Sharpe cannot.

For the same portfolio, take the hypothetical benchmark $b = [1.5,\ 0,\ 1.5,\ 0.5,\ 2.0,\ 1.5,\ 0,\ 1.0]$ (mean $1.0\%$). Active returns $r - b = [2.0, -1.5, 1.0, -1.0, 2.5, -1.0, 1.5, 0.5]$ have mean $0.5\%$; deviations from that mean are $[1.5, -2, 0.5, -1.5, 2, -1.5, 1, 0]$, squaring to $2.25+4+0.25+2.25+4+2.25+1+0 = 16$; tracking error $= \sqrt{16/7} \approx 1.512\%$. So $\text{IR} = 0.5/1.512 \approx \textbf{0.33}$ monthly, or $\approx 1.15$ annualised ($0.33 \times \sqrt{12}$).

rows: Was the total risk taken efficiently?
Was the deviation from benchmark rewarded?

blocks.title: Short, lucky series
blocks.md: A Sharpe of 1.73 from eight months sounds excellent, but with so few observations the standard error of the volatility estimate alone is large. Hedge fund fact sheets quoting Sharpe from 24 monthly points routinely flatter reality; demand longer histories and out-of-sample evidence.

guidedExercise.prompt: A strategy produced monthly excess returns over the risk-free rate of $[1.0, -0.5, 2.0, 0.5]\%$. Compute the mean, the sample volatility ($n-1$), and the monthly Sharpe ratio.
hints: Divide the sum of squared deviations by $3$ here (four observations).

independentExercise.prompt: Monthly returns: $[4.0, -2.0, 1.0, -3.0, 2.0]\%$ with $r_f = 0.5\%$ per month and MAR $= 0.5\%$. Compute (a) the mean excess return, (b) the downside deviation (divide by $n = 5$), (c) the Sortino ratio, and (d) compare qualitatively with the Sharpe ratio you would expect for this series.
hints: Excess return is return minus 0.5 for every month.
Only months below MAR contribute to $\sigma_D$.
independentExercise.solution: (a) Excess returns: $[3.5, -2.5, 0.5, -3.5, 1.5]$; mean $= -0.5/5 = -0.10\%$. (b) Months below MAR: $-2.5$ and $-3.5$; squared shortfalls $6.25 + 12.25 = 18.5$; $\sigma_D = \sqrt{18.5/5} = \sqrt{3.7} \approx 1.924\%$. (c) Sortino $= -0.10/1.924 \approx -0.05$: negative, because the mean excess return is negative, no ratio can rescue a losing strategy. (d) The Sharpe would also be negative and smaller in magnitude than the Sortino's absolute value, since total volatility exceeds downside deviation.

commonMistakes: Comparing a monthly Sharpe with an annual one without scaling by $\sqrt{12}$ - always align frequencies first.
Using total volatility in a Sortino calculation (or downside deviation in a Sharpe), they answer different questions.
Computing tracking error from benchmark-relative returns but forgetting to subtract the benchmark mean in the numerator.
Trusting Sharpe on highly skewed strategies (e.g. short-volatility) where volatility understates tail risk.
realWorldApplication: Institutional allocators screen thousands of funds with exactly these ratios, typically demanding multi-year Sharpe above some threshold and IR above ~0.5 for active managers; the ratios are computed by the same risk systems you will build.
quantFinanceApplication: A performance engine ingests daily returns, aligns them with benchmark series, computes rolling 12-month Sharpe/Sortino/IR and flags any strategy whose ratio degrades beyond control limits.
summary: Sharpe $= (\bar{R} - r_f)/\sigma$: reward per unit of total volatility; annualise by $\sqrt{f}$.
Sortino replaces total volatility with downside deviation below MAR, so upside volatility is not penalised.
Information ratio = mean active return / tracking error; it is the Sharpe ratio of benchmark-relative performance.
All three ratios assume returns are well-behaved; skewed or fat-tailed strategies need tail-aware measures too.

quiz.prompt: Mean excess return $1.0\%$ per month, monthly volatility $2.0\%$. What is the annualised Sharpe ratio? Round to 2 decimals.
Which ratio would you quote when comparing a fund to its stated benchmark rather than to cash?
quiz.explanation: The information ratio divides mean *active* return (over the benchmark) by tracking error, it is the natural benchmark-relative measure.

quiz.prompt: Monthly returns $[2.0, -1.0, 3.0, 0.0]\%$, MAR $= 0\%$. Compute the downside deviation (divide by $n = 4$) in %, to 2 decimals.
quiz.explanation: Only the month below MAR contributes: squared shortfall $(-1.0)^2 = 1$. Mean squared shortfall $= 1/4 = 0.25$, so $\sigma_D = \sqrt{0.25} = 0.50\%$.

quiz.prompt: A strategy earns steady small gains with rare huge losses. Its Sharpe ratio will most likely:
options: Overstate risk-adjusted quality because volatility misses the tail
Understate quality because of the losses
Be unaffected by the loss distribution
quiz.explanation: Rare huge losses barely raise the standard deviation of a mostly-calm series, so Sharpe looks good while the tail risk is severe, a classic short-volatility signature.

quiz.prompt: Mean active return $0.5\%$ per month with tracking error $1.5\%$ per month: annualised information ratio to 2 decimals.
State one thing the Sharpe ratio ignores that the Sortino ratio addresses, and one thing both ignore that matters for risk.
quiz.modelAnswer: Sharpe penalises upside volatility while Sortino counts only downside deviations below MAR; both ignore higher moments, skewness and tail shape, so severe left-tail risk can hide behind a good ratio.
quiz.explanation: Sortino fixes the upside-volatility objection; neither ratio sees skew or kurtosis, so both can flatter strategies with rare catastrophic losses.

flashcards.back: $S = (\bar{R} - r_f)/\sigma$; annualise by multiplying by $\sqrt{f}$ for $f$ periods per year.

flashcards.front: Key weakness all three ratios share
flashcards.back: They summarise risk with one (or one-sided) volatility number and ignore skew/kurtosis, fat left tails can hide behind a high ratio.
